name: Right cylinder
seoDesc: Right cylinder: work out radius (r) from the surface to volume ratio. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Right cylinder calculator is a free, no-sign-up math tool. Fill in the 1 field it asks for and it works out radius (r) straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Right cylinder calculator work?
sections.html:
The Right cylinder calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports radius (r) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the surface to volume ratio (A / V).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Right cylinder calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Radius (r)=-1 ÷ 2 × height (h) + (1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (PI × (height (h) ^ 2) + 2 × total surface area (A)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Radius (r)=the square root of (volume (V) ÷ height (h)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Lateral surface area (A_l)=2 × PI × height (h) × radius (r)
Radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of ((longest diagonal (d) − height (h)) × (longest diagonal (d) + height (h)))
Radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × the square root of (base surface area (A_b)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Total surface area (A)=surface to volume ratio (A ÷ V) × volume (V)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Volume, opening in cubic centimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Right cylinder calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the surface to volume ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Right cylinder calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns radius (r), derived from the surface to volume ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Right cylinder calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the surface to volume ratio, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter radius (r) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Radius (r) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Right cylinder calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
